newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: BOND SENTENCED TO ANOTHER FOUR YEARS JAIL
Former tycoon Alan Bond has been sentenced to four years jail for his part in the nation's biggest case of corporate fraud.
The sentence will start at the end of his current three year term for another set of fraud offences - his earliest release date for that is August this year.
Bond pleaded guilty to two charges of failing to act honestly as a company director in the late 1980s.
The charges relate to the transfer of one Billion dollars from Bell Resources to Bond Corporation.
Bond will be eligible for parole which means he will serve at least 16 months of the four year term.
CHARLEVILLE PEOPLE RETURNING HOME
In the south-west Queensland town of Charleville, at least half of the nearly 800 people forced to leave their homes because of flooding have returned to their houses.
Emergency service organisations have launched a clean-up plan as floodwaters, caused when the Warrego River burst its banks, recede.
Some people have to wait in emergency accommodation until power is restored to their residence or flooding drops.
Extra fire hoses are being brought in to clean mud from homes, State Government officers are assessing the damage bill, and trauma counsellors are on hand to help victims.
The SES director, Ken Callum, says the risk of an outbreak of disease is low.
AUSSIES GAMBLE BILLIONS OF DOLLARS
The Australian love of a bet is worth more than seven and a half billion dollars a year.
A Bureau of Statistics survey of Australia's gambling industries says poker and gaming machines account for just over half of all net takings.
Lotteries, including lotto, accounted for 18 percent of gambling takings.
On and off-course betting accounted for a similar figures while the casino gaming tables took 13 percent of the amount bet in Australia.
NEW LAWS NEEDED TO MAKE INTERNET TRADE A SUCCESS
The Australian Law Reform Commission says the federal government must remove legal uncertainties over Internet trade so business can take advantage of the technology.
Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says he's committed to enacting regulations to ensure Australia can globalise its markets.
Commission president Alan Rose says businesses aren't using electronic means of commerce because of a lack of security and privacy.
He says certainty in electronic commerce depends on government commitment to clearing up the grey areas with legislation.
BUDGET CUTS SHOULD FALL ON WELFARE: FARMERS FEDERATION
The National Farmers' Federation says it's time for the government to cut welfare spending.
It has urged the Coalition not to make the mistake of avoiding politically-difficult social welfare cuts in this year's budget.
The farming lobby says the rural sector made a significant contribution to fiscal tightening last year and further taxes or cuts will limit innovation and production.
The NFF has continued its call for wide-ranging tax reform, including broadening the indirect and income tax bases.
HALF OF REPUBLIC CONVENTION SHOULD BE WOMEN-ELECTORAL LOBBY
The Women's Electoral Lobby has called on the federal government to make sure half of the delegates to the convention on the republic are women.
The lobby says there were no women at the convention leading up to Federation, but says there must be equal represenatation at this year's forum.
The convention is planned for November or December this year, and will discuss the republic and other constitutional reforms.
RUM WHIFF POSTERS WITHDRAWN AFTER PROTESTS
The controversial new alcohol promotion using aromatic posters in bus shelters has been ditched
The bus shelter posters involving a non-alcohol lemon essence promped wide-spread community and government condemnation.
The company, Baccardi-Martini Pacific, says the outcry over the advertisements has forced them withdraw all the posters and abandon the national campaign.
